record.original_question: Call a body V in R^3 an optical fiber if it is bounded by two plane figures F1 and F2 together with a smooth tube Σ, and every light ray entering V through one end and reflecting perfectly on the interior walls exits through the other end with probability 1, while every light ray starting inside V exits through one of the ends with probability 1. Must every such optical fiber admit a slicing into plane figures that meet the walls at right angles?

evidence.quote: Suppose that V is a body in R^3 bounded by two plane figures F1 and F2 (the ends) and a smooth surface Σ (a tube). Suppose that a light ray entering V thru one end and bouncing with perfect reflection from the interior walls of Σ will emerge from the other end with probability 1; moreover, a light ray that emerges from the interior of V, after bouncing, emerges from one of the ends with probability 1. In this case, we say that V is an optical fiber.
Is it always possible to slice an optical fiber into plane figures that meet the walls at right angles?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define an optical fiber to be a body V ⊂ ℝ³ whose boundary is the union of two plane regions F₁ and F₂ (called the ends) and a smooth surface Σ (called the tube), and which satisfies the following two reflective transport conditions for billiard trajectories of light (straight-line motion inside V with specular reflection off Σ):

(i) A light ray that enters V through one of the ends F_i, undergoing perfect specular reflection on Σ at every encounter, exits V through the other end with probability 1 (with respect to the natural measure on incoming directions and entry points).

(ii) A light ray emanating from any interior point of V, in any direction, exits V through one of the two ends F₁, F₂ with probability 1.

Question: Must every optical fiber V admit a slicing by a one-parameter family of plane cross-sections (foliating V from F₁ to F₂) such that each cross-section is a plane figure meeting the tube Σ orthogonally along its boundary?
